items.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I didn't have a real rude awakening until I was told by a conductor, one of the guest conductors, he'd love to have me in his orchestra but he thought that the board of directors where he had the orchestra were not ready to accept an African American

ctx.x: So that gave me definite proof that it's possible. Then when the orchestra had some students fill in for the orchestra because of whatever reasons … they wanted the students to do that, I was one of the bass players that was in the orchestra for my senior year in college. So it seemed to me that those options were still available. I didn't have a real rude awakening until I was told by a conductor, one of the guest conductors, he'd love to have me in his orchestra but he thought that the board of directors where…
And that was a major maestro that told you that.

items.title: Ron Carter interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: And Leopold Stokowski, who was one of the guest conductors of the Philharmonic when I was there, took me aside when he was there for the one week

ctx.x: Right at that time, when you were about to graduate from Eastman, what were your career aspirations then?

Well I thought that making gigs is one thing, you know twenty bucks a night and you play your brains out and have a great time, but I wasn’t sure that that’s what I wanted to do. And seeing what appeared to be a relatively stable financial environment as classical orchestral playing, I said well I’ll spend four years here and this is my last two weeks at school I might as well find out what the deal is. And Leopold Stokowski, who was one of the guest conductors of the Philharmonic when I was there, took me aside…
And the young black musician nowadays is not going to be encouraged to go that route anyway.
